title: 001 — GPT-6.1 Sol: OpenAI's mid-tier model for coding, agents and computer use
html:
001 — GPT-6.1 Sol: OpenAI's mid-tier model for coding, agents and computer use

The one idea: GPT-6.1 Sol is the middle model of OpenAI's GPT-6 family. OpenAI positions it close to the top model (GPT-6 Astra) on coding, computer use and professional work at a fifth of Astra's token price, which makes it the sensible default for most agent and coding workloads.

Added 2026-10-05 · Released 2026-09-29 by OpenAI

1. What it is

GPT-6.1 Sol replaces GPT-6 Sol as the middle tier of the GPT-6 family. The API model ID is gpt-6.1-sol. It is available in the OpenAI API, and in ChatGPT Work and Codex for paid plans. At launch it was not yet in the plain Chat experience.

The family now has three tiers, and the choice between them is mostly a cost-versus-capability call:

Model Price per 1M tokens (input / output) OpenAI's positioning
GPT-6 Astra $10 / $50 Most intelligent, for the hardest reasoning work
GPT-6.1 Sol $2 / $10 (cached input $0.10) Near-Astra intelligence for complex coding, research and computer use
GPT-6 Luna $0.10 / $0.50 Fast and cheap, for focused, repeated tasks such as extraction or classification

OpenAI also announced an "ultrafast" variant of Sol, with up to 8x faster token generation, as coming soon after launch.

2. Why it matters

  • Price point for agents. Coding and computer-use agents burn many tokens per task because they read files, call tools and loop. Near-top quality at a fifth of the top model's price changes which of these workloads are affordable to run all day.
  • Caching makes long sessions cheap. Cached input is $0.10 per million tokens, 95% below the standard input price. Agents resend the same instructions, tool definitions and repository context on every turn, so a well-ordered prompt pays mostly the cached rate.
  • Multi-agent work is built in (beta). OpenAI's guide says Sol can hand independent work to subagents, for example investigating different parts of a codebase in parallel.
  • Better alignment results than GPT-6 Sol, according to OpenAI's evaluations, which matters when the model acts on your systems rather than just answering.

It is not the best model at everything: OpenAI says it stays below Astra on most benchmarks and frames it as the model for everyday work, not the hardest problems.

3. How it works

From a developer's point of view, three dials decide cost and quality:

  1. Model tier: Luna, Sol or Astra.
  2. Reasoning effort: how much the model thinks before answering. The GPT-6 Sol model docs list none, low, medium (the default), high, xhigh and max. OpenAI's guide maps them roughly as: low for routine extraction, medium for work that needs judgement, high for hard debugging, and the top levels only when high falls short. Effort can be changed mid-conversation without breaking the cache.
  3. Context management: prompt caching (put stable instructions first, changing details last) and compaction, which shrinks a long conversation while keeping the state needed to continue.
---
title: GPT-6.1 Sol — choosing tier and effort
---
flowchart LR
    T["Task"] --> Q{"Repeated, narrow task?"}
    Q -- yes --> L["GPT-6 Luna<br/>low effort"]
    Q -- no --> H{"Hardest reasoning,<br/>cost no object?"}
    H -- yes --> A["GPT-6 Astra"]
    H -- no --> S["GPT-6.1 Sol<br/>medium effort"]
    S --> E{"Result good enough?"}
    E -- no --> S2["Raise effort<br/>(high, then xhigh)"]
    E -- yes --> D["Ship it"]

4. How to use it

Use the Responses API (v1/responses). The GPT-6 Sol docs say that built-in tools and function calling belong there, and that Chat Completions supports function calling only with reasoning effort set to none.

A minimal request:

curl https://api.openai.com/v1/responses \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "gpt-6.1-sol",
    "reasoning": { "effort": "medium" },
    "input": "Review this C# method for thread-safety issues: ..."
  }'

The same call from C# with a plain HttpClient, so it does not depend on any SDK version:

using System.Net.Http.Json;

using var http = new HttpClient { BaseAddress = new Uri("https://api.openai.com/") };
http.DefaultRequestHeaders.Authorization =
    new("Bearer", Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("OPENAI_API_KEY"));

var request = new
{
    model = "gpt-6.1-sol",
    reasoning = new { effort = "medium" },
    input = "Summarise the risks in this deployment plan: ..."
};

using HttpResponseMessage response = await http.PostAsJsonAsync("v1/responses", request);
response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
Console.WriteLine(await response.Content.ReadAsStringAsync());

The request shape follows OpenAI's Responses API. The model ID and effort values come from the announcement and model docs. Check the API reference for the response format before parsing it.

In practice:

  • Keep the system prompt, tool definitions and long reference material at the start of the input, and the per-task details at the end. That keeps the cacheable prefix stable.
  • Start at medium. Raise to high only for tasks where you can see quality fail, and drop to low for extraction-style steps.
  • For a pipeline of many narrow calls (classify, extract, route), try Luna first. It costs a twentieth of Sol's price.

5. Trade-offs and limits

  • Not the top model: OpenAI says it is below GPT-6 Astra on most benchmarks.
  • Context window: the announcement does not state it. The GPT-6 Sol model page lists 1,050,000 input tokens and 128,000 output tokens. Check the GPT-6.1 Sol page before relying on the same limits.
  • Cost at high effort: higher reasoning effort means more output tokens. At $10 per million output tokens, xhigh on every call adds up quickly.
  • Vendor lock-in: prompts tuned to one model's effort levels and caching behaviour do not transfer cleanly to another provider. Keep the model behind an interface so you can swap or route between models.
  • Multi-agent features are beta, so expect behaviour and pricing details to change.

6. Where it fits

  • LLM engineering and RAG: prompting, caching, evaluation and cost control.
  • AI in the SDLC: coding agents and how to review their work.
  • AI and ML foundations: what reasoning models are doing under the hood.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. Your agent sends a 40,000-token repository summary on every turn. How should you order the prompt so most of those tokens bill at the cached rate?
  2. When would GPT-6 Luna be a better choice than GPT-6.1 Sol, even though Sol is smarter?
  3. Chat Completions supports function calling only with reasoning effort none. What does that mean for which API a tool-using agent should be built on?
  4. You raised reasoning effort from medium to xhigh and quality barely changed. What do you check next?
  5. How would you design your code so that switching from Sol to another model is a configuration change?
